outline.title: Abstract
outline.description: A concise summary of the survey, highlighting the rapid evolution of LLM security threats and defenses between 2023 and 2026. It will outline the shift from unimodal, static vulnerabilities to complex, multimodal, and agentic attack vectors. The abstract will summarize the four core pillars of the survey: data/model poisoning, prompt injection, adversarial attacks, and hallucinations, concluding with a call for dynamic, co-evolutionary defense mechanisms.

outline.title: 1. Introduction
outline.description: This section establishes the motivation, scope, and contributions of the survey. It will detail the chronological evolution of LLM security from 2023 to 2026, illustrating how the field transitioned from identifying baseline vulnerabilities in isolated models to addressing a sophisticated adversarial arms race in multimodal and agentic systems. It will clearly define the scope of the survey, encompassing training-time threats (poisoning), inference-time threats (prompt injection, adversarial attacks), and reliability issues (hallucinations).

outline.title: 2. Background and Preliminaries
outline.description: Provides the foundational concepts and terminology required for the survey. It will define key terms such as Jailbreak, Prompt Injection (Direct/Indirect), Attack Success Rate (ASR), Safety Alignment (RLHF, DPO), and Red Teaming. The section will outline the standard LLM architecture and deployment pipeline, establishing a comprehensive threat model that categorizes vulnerabilities into training-time (e.g., Data Poisoning, Backdoor Attacks) and inference-time vectors.

outline.title: 3. Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning
outline.description: Analyzes the evolution of data and model poisoning from 2024 to 2025. It will discuss the initial benchmarking of generative backdoors in open-source models like LLaMA-2, Mistral, and GPT-J, referencing foundational frameworks by [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking] and [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. The section will then detail the critical transition from unimodal text vulnerabilities to complex multimodal and embodied AI attack vectors, specifically highlighting the exploitation of alignment mechanisms (e.g., RLHF pipelines) and retrieval systems in late 2024 and 2025.

outline.title: 4. Inference-Time Threats I: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
outline.description: Examines the rapid transformation of prompt injection and jailbreak attacks between 2025 and 2026. It will document the shift from static, rule-based bypasses to automated, co-evolutionary adversarial optimization. The section will detail state-of-the-art offensive techniques, including modified Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) fuzzing, and genetic algorithms, noting their ability to achieve 50% to 71% ASR against advanced LLM agents as demonstrated by [Zhan_2025_LLM], [Wang_2025_LLM], and [Maloyan_2025_LLM].

outline.title: 5. Inference-Time Threats II: Adversarial Attacks
outline.description: Explores the landscape of adversarial attacks on LLMs and MLLMs from 2024 to 2026. It will cover the identification of domain-specific vulnerabilities, particularly in high-stakes sectors like healthcare, referencing [Yang_2024_Adversarial] and the manipulation of sensitive datasets like MIMIC-III. The section will also discuss the evolution of early defensive wrappers, such as the contrastive prompt tuning introduced by [Wang_2024_Advqdet] for detecting query-based black-box attacks, and how these patchwork defenses evolved into a sophisticated arms race.

outline.title: 6. Model Reliability: LLM Hallucinations and Factual Consistency
outline.description: Traces the conceptual maturation of hallucination detection and mitigation from 2023 to 2026. It will begin with the 2023 baseline of using LLMs as evaluators via zero-shot inference-time methods, highlighting ChainPoll [Friel_2023_LLM] and its use of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting to drastically reduce inference costs. The narrative will then progress to the 2024 shift away from treating non-factual generations as binary errors, moving toward mechanistically informed and conceptually nuanced frameworks for factual consistency.

outline.title: 8. Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: Provides a holistic overview of defense mechanisms spanning the categorized threats. It will detail the transition from early 'patchwork' defenses (e.g., contrastive prompt tuning achieving 99% detection [Wang_2024_Advqdet]) to modern, dynamic ensemble systems. Topics include perplexity filters, input sanitization, robust RLHF alignment, and the bifurcation in 2025 toward either extreme computational efficiency or highly dynamic, co-evolutionary defensive architectures designed to counter automated MCTS and GCG attacks.

outline.title: 7. Testing Methodologies and Evaluation
outline.description: A mandatory, dedicated section synthesizing benchmarks, datasets, metrics, and evaluation frameworks across all security categories. It will cover Attack Success Rate (ASR) measurement for prompt injection (referencing the 50-71% ASR metrics from [Zhan_2025_LLM, Wang_2025_LLM, Maloyan_2025_LLM]), domain-specific datasets like MIMIC-III for adversarial robustness [Yang_2024_Adversarial], frameworks for evaluating generative backdoors [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking, Li_2024_Backdoorllm], and computational cost metrics for hallucination detection (e.g., ChainPoll's efficiency [Friel_2023_LLM]). It will critique the current reliance on static benchmarks and advocate for dynamic red-teaming tools.

outline.title: 9. Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: Synthesizes the gaps and limitations in the current LLM security landscape. It will discuss the fundamental asymmetry between attackers (who leverage automated, low-cost fuzzing) and defenders (who rely on computationally expensive guardrails). The section will highlight open challenges such as securing multimodal agents, the theoretical limits of safety alignment, and the need for standardized, evolving benchmarks that do not suffer from data contamination.

outline.title: 10. Conclusion
outline.description: Summarizes the core findings of the survey, reiterating the rapid escalation of LLM security threats from 2023 to 2026. It will provide practical recommendations for researchers and practitioners, emphasizing the necessity of integrating security at the architectural level rather than relying on post-hoc wrappers, and calling for continued investment in dynamic, mechanistically informed defense strategies.
